procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Allahabad High Court dated April 16, 1968, in Criminal Misc. Case No. 3403 of 1967, quashing the proceedings initiated in the Court of Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Nainital.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Brij Mohan Chandra applied to the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad under s. 561A, Cr. P.C. for quashing the proceedings in the court of Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Nainital. The High Court (S. D. Singh J) on April 16, 1968 quashed the proceedings by the impugned order holding that cl. (vii) of s. 128(1) of the Municipalities Act did not authorise the levy of toll-tax on passengers and that a connected notification also levied tax only on vehicles and not on passengers.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Municipal Board, Nainital, and the Executive Officer of the Board appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision.

decision.appeal_result: this appeal fails and is dismissed

issue.issue_text: Whether a toll imposed on a vehicle entering a municipality could legally be realised from the passengers carried by it because of their nexus with the entry of the vehicle.

facts: A toll tax was levied on vehicles entering the Nainital Municipality.
The law and relevant notifications specified that the tax was imposed on the vehicles, not on the passengers.
The rules expressly made the "person-in-charge" of the vehicle liable for paying the toll.
law: The appellants argued for a "nexus theory," contending that since the passengers have a connection with the entry of the vehicle, the toll could be legally collected from them.
The Court noted that there was no legal provision, precedent, or principle that made passengers liable for a toll imposed on the vehicle they were travelling in.
application: The Court rejected the "nexus theory," reasoning that applying it in this case would erase the legal distinction between a tax on vehicles and a tax on passengers.
It emphasized that the liability was clearly and specifically fixed on the person-in-charge of the vehicle, not the passengers.
Since no law made the passengers liable, the Court found no basis for the municipality to demand the toll from them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the toll tax imposed on a vehicle could not be legally collected from its passengers. The liability to pay the tax rests solely with the person in charge of the vehicle, as specified by the law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the imposition of a tax on passengers was competent under the clause that speaks of a toll on vehicles and other conveyances.

facts: A municipality imposed a toll under a clause that authorized a "toll on vehicles and other conveyances... entering the municipality."
The municipality attempted to collect this toll from the passengers traveling in the vehicles, not just from the vehicle operator.
The appellants argued that the toll on the vehicle could be legally collected from the passengers due to the "nexus" between the passengers and the vehicle's entry into the municipality.
law: The relevant legal clause (s. 128 (1) (vii)) authorizes a toll on "vehicles and other conveyances," not on passengers.
The rules for collecting the toll specified that the tax on laden vehicles was payable by the "person-in-charge" of the vehicle.
application: The Court found the language of the authorizing clause to be "clear and unambiguous" in that it only permitted a tax on vehicles, not the passengers within them.
The Court rejected the "nexus theory," stating that accepting it would erase the distinction between a vehicle tax and a passenger tax.
The Court noted that the appellants themselves conceded they had never intended to impose a tax directly on passengers.
The Court found no legal provision, precedent, or principle that would make passengers liable for a tax that was legally imposed on the vehicle.
Since the law and its associated rules explicitly made the "person-in-charge" of the vehicle liable for the toll, there was no basis to demand payment from the passengers.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the imposition of a tax on passengers was incompetent and ultra vires (beyond the legal power) of the clause, as the clause only authorized a toll on vehicles. The attempt to collect the vehicle toll from passengers was therefore illegal.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 164 of the Act could operate to bar the jurisdiction of the High Court to quash a levy that was outside the Act and ultra vires the taxing power of the Board.

facts: The appellants' counsel argued that Section 164 of the Act acted as a bar to the High Court's jurisdiction, preventing it from entertaining the petition and declaring the levy illegal.
law: A provision within an Act that bars a court's jurisdiction cannot operate if the action being challenged (in this case, a tax levy) is itself outside the scope of that Act and beyond the legal power (ultra vires) of the authority that imposed it.
application: The Court reasoned that the appellants' argument ignored the "vital point" that the levy in question was found to be "outside the Act" and "ultra vires" the taxing power of the Board.
Because the levy was fundamentally unauthorized by the Act, a section *within* that same Act (Section 164) could not be used to shield the illegal levy from judicial review.
The Court stated that the High Court's jurisdiction to quash proceedings relating to an ultra vires levy cannot be taken away to the prejudice of an aggrieved citizen.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that Section 164 of the Act could not operate to bar the High Court's jurisdiction because the levy itself was outside the Act and ultra vires the Board's taxing power. The submission was accordingly "repelled".

arguments.issue_text: Whether a toll imposed on a vehicle entering a municipality could legally be realised from the passengers carried by it because of their nexus with the entry of the vehicle.
appellant_arguments: The toll imposed on a vehicle could legally be realised from the passengers it carries because of the nexus between the passengers and the entry of the vehicle.
This approach is supported by the policy of the law to ensure the collection of taxes by preventing fraudulent evasion.
respondent_arguments: The nexus theory cannot be applied to enable the Municipal Board to recover a toll-tax on vehicles from the passengers travelling in them.
There is no provision of law that makes passengers liable to pay a toll-tax that is specifically imposed on vehicles.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the imposition of a tax on passengers was competent under the clause that speaks of a toll on vehicles and other conveyances.
appellant_arguments: The appellant initially attempted to justify the levy under a different clause (cl. (xiv)) but abandoned this argument.
The appellant conceded and did not dispute that the relevant clause, which speaks of a toll on vehicles, does not authorize a tax on passengers.
respondent_arguments: The clause in question clearly and unambiguously speaks of a toll on vehicles, conveyances, animals, and laden coolies.
The clause does not include passengers, and therefore, the imposition of a tax on passengers by the Municipal Board is incompetent under this clause.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 164 of the Act could operate to bar the jurisdiction of the High Court to quash a levy that was outside the Act and ultra vires the taxing power of the Board.
appellant_arguments: Section 164 of the Act bars the jurisdiction of the High Court from entertaining the petition and reviewing the levy.
respondent_arguments: A jurisdictional bar like Section 164 does not apply when the levy in question is outside the scope of the Act and ultra vires the taxing power of the Board.
The High Court's jurisdiction to quash a levy that is ultra vires cannot be taken away to the prejudice of an aggrieved citizen.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A toll tax imposed on a vehicle cannot be legally recovered from the passengers travelling in it when the governing law and rules explicitly fix the liability for payment on the person-in-charge of the vehicle. The theory of nexus cannot be applied to extend tax liability to persons not designated by the law as being responsible for its payment.
obiter: The jurisdiction of the High Court to quash proceedings relating to a levy which is ultra vires the taxing power of a Board cannot be taken away.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A toll-tax that is legally imposed on a vehicle cannot be demanded or realized from the passengers travelling in that vehicle. The court found no provision of law, precedent, or principle to support the submission that merely because passengers were carried by a vehicle, they could be held liable for a tax imposed on the vehicle's entry into a municipality. The 'nexus' theory is inapplicable for transferring such liability, and any rules for collection are irrelevant if the underlying tax was not competently imposed on the party from whom collection is sought.
legal_tests_applied: Ultra Vires Doctrine: The court examined whether the levy was outside the scope of the Act and beyond the taxing power of the Board. A jurisdictional bar within a statute cannot operate to protect a levy that is ultra vires the powers granted by that same statute.

Statutory Interpretation: The court analyzed the plain and unambiguous language of the authorizing clause, which speaks of a toll on 'vehicles' and other conveyances, to determine that it does not include passengers within its scope.
why_appellant_lost: The authorizing clause of the Act speaks in clear and unambiguous terms of a toll on vehicles, not passengers, a point the appellant did not dispute.
The court rejected the 'nexus' theory, stating it was difficult to apply it in a manner that would enable the Municipal Board to recover a toll-tax on vehicles from the passengers travelling in them.
The appellant could not point to any provision of law, precedent, or principle under which passengers could be held liable to pay a toll-tax that was specifically imposed on vehicles.
The collection rules cited by the appellant were unhelpful, as the rule concerning payment by a passenger presupposes that a toll has been validly imposed on passengers, which it had not.
The jurisdictional bar in Section 164 of the Act could not prevent the High Court from quashing the levy because the levy was outside the Act and ultra vires the Board's taxing power.
why_respondent_won: The clause authorizing the toll clearly speaks of a toll on vehicles and does not include passengers, making the imposition of a tax on passengers incompetent under that clause.
There is no provision of law that makes passengers liable to pay a toll-tax that is specifically imposed on vehicles.
A jurisdictional bar like Section 164 does not apply when the levy in question is outside the scope of the Act and ultra vires the taxing power of the Board.
policy_considerations: The court rejected the appellant's argument that the collection method was justified by the policy of the law to ensure the collection of taxes by preventing fraudulent evasion.
The court affirmed that the jurisdiction of the High Court to quash a levy which is ultra vires the taxing power of the Board cannot be taken away to the prejudice of the aggrieved citizen.
